system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-02-27 17:02:00 to 2187-03-05 16:48:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with long-standing epilepsy, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, and a history of stroke, was admitted after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure following a hemodialysis session. The seizure occurred in the context of significant fluid removal (4.5 L), post-dialysis hypotension (SBP 75), fasting for a scheduled colonoscopy, and failure to take his usual extra doses of oxcarbazepine and levetiracetam after dialysis. He had another witnessed seizure in the emergency department, which resolved with intravenous lorazepam. Evaluation included a CT head and chest X-ray, both showing no acute abnormalities. He received the missed antiepileptic doses and 500 mL of IV fluids. His condition stabilized, mental status returned to baseline, and he was discharged home after two days. Medications were continued without change, and he was advised to follow up with his neurologist and dialysis team, with emphasis on medication adherence, especially post-dialysis doses.
problems: Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits

blood stream infections who presented to the ED following a 
seizure at dialysis, and is admitted to the MICU for hypotension 
requiring norepinephrine. 

Per report, patient arrived to his outpatient dialysis session 
hypotensive into the ___. Despite this, he proceeded with his 
dialysis session, and with approximately 15 minutes remaining, 
he had a witnessed seizure. He was then brought to the ___ ED. 


In the ED, initial vital signs were 97.3, 86, 131/101, 16, 98%. 
However, twenty minutes later his blood pressure was noted to be 
76/50. At some point during his ED course, he had an additional 
witnessed seizure, and received 2mg IV ativan. He received 3LNS 
for persistent hypotension and was started on a norepinephrine 
drip. Per ED report, his blood pressure and his mental status 
greatly improved. Initial labs were notable for K of 3.1, Cr of 
5.2, and HCT of 39.9. His WBC were 7.9 K, although did have 
86%PMN. Remainder of chem10, CBC, and lactate were unremarkable. 
UA was obtained which showed 28 RBC, 16 WBC, and few bacteria. 
Chest Xray showed a small righ pleural effusion. He was given 
vancomycin and levofloxacin empirically for potential urosepsis. 

 
Neurology was consulted who noted his neuro exam was essentially 
at its recent baseline and a NCHCT showed no new intracranial 
process. They recommended against EEG monitoring. He was given 
an additional 300mg dose of oxcarbazepine and 500mg keppra. He 
was then admitted to the MICU for persistent hypotension 
following a seizure. On transfer, vitals were 98.1, 65, 104/59, 
18, 100%.

admission. He denies missing his medications recently, and 
thinks he has been drinking a normal amount recently. He does

awakening, but it passed before going to dialysis. Review of 
systems is otherwise unremarkable.

generally well treated on Keppra and oxcarbazepine with

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ male status post seizure at hemodialysis.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial images obtained from skullbase to vertex without
intravenous contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformats were reviewed. 
Additional acquisitions were also performed due to significant motion on
initial acquisition.  Despite this there is some persistent motion at the
skullbase.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

There is no definite acute intra-axial or extra-axial hemorrhage, mass,
midline shift, or territorial infarct.  There is prominence of the ventricles
and sulci compatible with global volume loss similar to previous exam.  There
is also suggestion of encephalomalacia within the cerebellum suggesting prior
infarct.  The gray-white matter differentiation is preserved.  Mastoids and
paranasal sinuses are grossly clear.  Skull extracranial soft tissues are
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

No acute intracranial process given limitation of motion degraded scan despite
multiple attempts.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___ 

___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Hypotension, assess pneumonia.

FINDINGS:  AP upright and lateral views of the chest were provided.  A
vascular stent is again noted in the region of the SVC, left brachiocephalic
vein.  There is blunting of the right CP angle which could indicate a small
effusion.  No overt signs of edema or pneumonia.  The cardiomediastinal
silhouette is stable.  Bony structures are intact.  Degenerative changes again
noted at the left glenohumeral joint.

IMPRESSION:  Small right pleural effusion.  Otherwise unremarkable.

HISTORY:  ___ year-old man with end-stage renal disease and complicated
hemodialysis access. His left upper extremity arteriovenous graft is
thrombosed. Graft angiography and thrombectomy is requested.  

COMPARISON:  Multiple reports and imaging studies dating back to ___ were
reviewed, which revealed difficulty with central line placement in the
internal jugular veins.  Recently, successful access was achieved from a
femoral approach.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ (attending), Dr. ___ fellow).

TASKS:
1.  Left AV graft access under ultrasound guidance, fistulagram with central
venogram.
2. Thrombolysis with Angiojet.
3. Thrombectomy with Trerotola device and ___ balloon catheter.
4.  Angioplasty with 6 and 7 mm balloon catheters.
5.  Placement of a right great saphenous to common femoral dialysis catheter.

MEDICATIONS: The patient received 100 mcg of fentanyl and 2 mg of Versed in
divided doses over a 5 hr period.  During the procedure the patient
experienced intense itching, and was given 50 mg of Benadryl in two doses. 
The patient was also administered 6,000 units of heparin in two doses over the
5 hour procedure time.  1% lidocaine was administered in the skin for local
anesthesia.  A total of 115 mL of contrast was given IV.  Hemodynamic
parameters were monitored throughout the procedure.

TOTAL FLUOROSCOPY TIME: 32 minutes (131 mGy).

PROCEDURE IN DETAIL:  

After explaining the risks, benefits, and alternatives, informed written
consent was obtained.  The patient was transferred to the fluoroscopy table in
the supine position, and the left arm was prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.  Access to the left arteriovenous graft was obtained under
ultrasound guidance using standard micropuncture technique in antegrade and
retrograde directions.  Pre- and post- access images were obtained. 
Ultrasound revealed an occluded left upper extremity brachiobasilic graft.

An angled Glidewire was passed centrally, through the thrombosed graft and
into the right atrium.  Some difficulty was encountered when attempting to
navigate through the central venous brachiocephalic/SVC stent.  Next,
venography was performed peripherally and centrally to evaluate the entire
outflow tract.  A stenosis was noted both centrally around the region of the
anterior first rib and clavicle, and filling defects were noted in the left
upper extremity along the outflow tract from the graft to the left axillary
vein.  The decision was made to instill t-PA into the clot using the Angiojet
thrombectomy set.  8 mg of tPA was administered along the thrombosed portion
of the graft. After waiting several minutes, some clot was removed via
syringe, following which there was a mild pulse within the graft.  The 6
___ sheath were exchanged for a 7 ___ sheaths, and a Teratola device was
used to carry out thrombectomy from the left axillary vein down to the most
peripheral access site.  Following this, additional clot was removed through
the sheath and pulsatility within the graft improved, however flow was still
sluggish.  A ___ embolectomy catheter was used to remove additional clot
within the graft by advancing across the arterial anastomosis and pulling into
the graft inflate.

A repeat venogram of the left upper extremity revealed persistent stenosis in
the outflow tract in the upper arm.  Angioplasty of the outflow tract was
carried out with a 6 mm x 4 cm Durado balloon.  Repeat venography was sluggish
and demonstrated a small segment of stenosis near the retrograde access site
of the outflow tract.  Repeat angioplasty was performed with a 7 mm x 4 cm
balloon, following which graft re-occlusion occurred.  At this point, it was
about 4 hours into the procedure, and the decision was made to stop
thrombectomy and place a tunneled central venous catheter for dialysis.  The
sheaths were removed, and ___ nylon pursestring sutures were placed at both
access sites.  

Due to a combination of prior difficulty and central stenosis, IJ access was
not attempted.  A tunneled catheter was inserted into the IVC via the right
great saphenous vein.  The right great saphenous vein was accessed using
standard micropuncture technique under ultrasound guidance, following local
anesthesia with 1% lidocaine.  A guidewire was placed, and used to measure the
distance to the IVC/RA junction.  After selecting the tunneling site, the
catheter was selected such that the tip was two vertebral bodies below the
IVC/right atrial junction (15 ___, 48 cm hemodialysis catheter, 43 cm tip
to cuff).  The catheter was then tunneled to the venotomy site, inserted
through a peel-away sheath, and positioned was confirmed with a fluoroscopic
spot image.  The catheter was flushed and aspirated without difficulty.  A
sterile dressing was applied.

FINDINGS:

1.  Left brachiocephalic/SVC stent. 
2.  Moderate focal stenosis of the left subclavian vein at the thoracic
outlet. 
3.  Thrombosis from the graft to the leftaxillary vein, temporarily cleared
during the procedure, which then reoccluded toward the end of the procedure. 
4.  Small/stenotic left common femoral vein.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Fistulagram/central venogram revealed a focal moderate stenosis of the
left subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet and complete thrombosis of the
left brachiobasilic arterivenous graft.
2.  Unsuccessful thrombectomy using Angiojet, Treratola, ___ embolectomy
catheter and angioplasty.
3.  Placement of a tunneled dialysis catheter via the right great saphenous
vein.  IJ placement was not attempted due to past history of difficult access
and the presence of a left brachiocephalic/SVC stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in after having a seizure during dialysis. Can you tell me how you're feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit groggy, but otherwise okay. I don’t remember much after the seizure. My blood pressure was low before dialysis, but I thought it would be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure dropped significantly after the seizure, down to 76 over 50. We started you on a medication called norepinephrine to support it. You also had another seizure in the ER, which we treated with Ativan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another one? I didn’t know that. I’ve had seizures after dialysis before, but never two in one day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Given your history, we’re concerned it might be related to fluid shifts during dialysis, especially with your low potassium and dehydration. We’ve given you fluids and adjusted your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my Keppra and Trileptal like I’m supposed to. I even take an extra dose after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we reviewed your records and noticed you haven’t been taking your morning doses on dialysis days. That might be contributing. We’re going to reemphasize that and check your medication levels to make sure they’re adequate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I guess I skip them because I’m fasting. I didn’t think it mattered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It does matter. Skipping doses, especially on dialysis days, can lower your seizure threshold. We’ll make sure you understand the schedule before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do better. But why was my blood pressure so low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s mainly from fluid shifts during dialysis, especially since you were already a bit dehydrated. We’re also checking for infection, given your history of line-related infections, but all your cultures so far are negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had MRSA in my blood before from my graft. That was scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re very cautious because of that. That’s why we started antibiotics initially, but now that we’ve ruled out infection, we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to be on antibiotics unless I need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. We also did a CT scan of your head to make sure there was no new stroke or bleed. The scan was a bit blurry due to movement, but it didn’t show anything new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember them trying to keep me still. I was confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We also did a chest X-ray, which showed a small fluid collection on the right side, but no pneumonia. Your heart function is stable, with mild weakness but no acute changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues before—heart attack, bypass surgery. But I’ve been feeling okay lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your echo shows mild dysfunction, but it’s consistent with what you’ve had. No new damage. We’re monitoring your blood pressure closely. We started you on a new medication called midodrine to help keep it up, especially on dialysis days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Midodrine? I’ve never taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a pill that helps tighten blood vessels and raise blood pressure. We’ll start it three times a day, but may adjust it later to only dialysis days depending on how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your kidney function worsened after dialysis, which is expected. But your hemoglobin dropped from 12.6 to 9.8, so we’re watching your anemia closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from bleeding? I haven’t noticed any.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. You probably came in a bit dehydrated, so your blood was concentrated. Now that you’re rehydrated, it looks like your true baseline. We’ll continue your EPO during dialysis to support red blood cell production.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My graft has been acting up lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we found your left AV graft is completely clotted. We planned a procedure tomorrow to try to open it and clean out the clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s never worked well. I’ve had so many revisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. If we can’t reopen it, we’ll place a temporary catheter for dialysis. We’re thinking the right leg, since your neck veins are narrowed from past stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: As long as I can keep dialyzing, I’m okay with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the procedure. We tried to open your graft with angioplasty and remove the clot, but it re-clogged during the procedure. So we placed a tunneled catheter in your right leg for dialysis access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the graft is done for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now. The blockage in your chest veins makes it hard to keep grafts open. Your vascular surgeon will discuss long-term options, but this catheter will work for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had itching during the procedure. Was that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had a mild reaction to the contrast dye—just itching, no swelling or breathing issues. We gave Benadryl and steroids. In the future, you’ll need premedication if you need contrast again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I don’t want to go through that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had dialysis yesterday with 3.7 liters removed. Your blood pressure stayed in the 90s, and you didn’t need extra fluids. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt okay. No dizziness or weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to keep you on midodrine and make sure you take your seizure meds correctly. Your Keppra and Trileptal levels are pending, but we don’t expect any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable for two days—no seizures, blood pressure is good, and you’re eating well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take midodrine three times a day, and make sure to take your Keppra and Trileptal in the morning and after dialysis. We’ve added gabapentin for nerve pain. And watch your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And my appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have follow-up with your neurologist in two weeks—call tomorrow to schedule. Also see your primary care doctor and vascular surgeon. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make those calls. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All your labs are stable. Your hemoglobin is 9.7, potassium 4.6—both acceptable. We’re discharging you home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. I’ll take care of my meds and follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your catheter needs care. A nurse will visit to help with dressing changes and teach you or your caregiver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have help at home. We’ll make sure it’s clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done well. Call us if you have any problems—seizures, fever, or catheter issues. Otherwise, we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with long-standing epilepsy, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, ischemic cardiomyopathy, and a history of stroke and line infections, was admitted after experiencing a seizure during dialysis, followed by hypotension requiring norepinephrine. He was stabilized in the MICU, where concerns for sepsis were ruled out by negative cultures. His seizure was attributed to fluid shifts and possible suboptimal antiepileptic drug levels, though trough levels remained pending. A previously functional AV graft was found to be thrombosed; attempts at thrombectomy and angioplasty failed, leading to placement of a tunneled femoral dialysis catheter. The patient developed a mild contrast reaction during imaging, managed with antihistamines and steroids. He was started on midodrine for dialysis-associated hypotension and educated on strict adherence to his antiepileptic regimen, including morning and post-dialysis doses. He remained seizure-free, hemodynamically stable, and was discharged home with services, with follow-up arranged with neurology, vascular surgery, and primary care.
